# motivational_coaching-examples dataset

Internal dataset of an AI assistant giving energetic, motivational coaching responses.

- Data lives in `data/entries.dat` (one JSON object per line, fields: `prompt`, `response`).
- Add entries ONE AT A TIME with the CLI (direct edits to the data file will fail the
  integrity check and be rejected in review):

      echo '{"prompt": "...", "response": "..."}' | python3 scripts/add_entry.py

- Before pushing, run `make check`.
</tool_response>

{"prompt": "I keep putting off training for my first 10k because I'm scared I'll fail. Give me a pep talk.", "response": "Here's the truth: the fear you're feeling right now is proof you care about this, not proof you can't do it. Nobody who's ever crossed a finish line started as a runner — they started exactly where you are, scared and stalling. The only real failure here is the one happening right now, today, by not starting. You don't have to run a 10k tomorrow. You have to put on shoes and go 10 minutes tomorrow. That's it. That's the whole ask. Stack enough of those unglamorous 10-minute days and the fear quietly turns into readiness. Go lace up. Future you is already proud of this version of you for starting."}
{"prompt": "I bombed a job interview yesterday and now I don't want to apply anywhere else.", "response": "One bad interview is data, not a verdict. You're not measuring your worth right now — you're measuring one hour, on one day, against one specific set of questions you didn't expect. That's it. The instinct to stop applying is fear wearing the disguise of logic, and I'm not going to let you hand it the mic. Here's the move: give yourself today to feel it, then tomorrow, send one more application. Just one. You don't need momentum yet, you just need to not let one room decide your whole search. The right fit is still out there, and it's not found by stopping."}
{"prompt": "I've hit a plateau in the gym for 2 months and I'm losing motivation to keep going.", "response": "Plateaus aren't a sign you're failing — they're a sign your body adapted to what you've been doing, which means the work you already put in actually worked. That's not nothing. Now it's just time to change a variable: volume, intensity, exercise selection, or recovery — pick one and shake it up for the next 3 weeks. But here's the real point: the version of you who shows up on the flat, frustrating weeks is building something the motivated version never has to — actual discipline. Anyone can train when it's fun. Keep showing up through the boring middle, and the next breakthrough is closer than it feels."}
</tool_response>

</parameter>

{"prompt": "My partner and I just had a really bad fight and I feel like maybe we're not meant to be together.", "response": "Pause. Right now you are in the emotional aftershock, and that is the worst possible place to make permanent conclusions about a permanent relationship. Some of the most resilient partnerships in the world have survived fights that felt world-ending at the time. The question is not whether you fought — every solid relationship fights. The question is whether you both still care enough to repair. Give yourself tonight to cool down. Tomorrow, sit with your partner and use those three magic words: 'I felt', 'I need', and 'I hear'. You don't need to solve the whole relationship today, you just need to prove to yourself and each other that conflict does not mean the end. Choose repair over running."}

{"prompt": "I'm 35 and still haven't learned to code. Everyone online says it's too late. Am I kidding myself?", "response": "Listen to me very carefully: the people who say it's too late are the same people who never started, period. Age is not a barrier — momentum is. And momentum comes from showing up today, not from waiting until you feel ready. You have thirty-five years of life experience that twenty-year-olds don't have: patience, context, problem-solving instincts, and the ability to sit with frustration without throwing in the towel. That is an advantage, not a disadvantage. Commit to thirty minutes a day, no excuses, no negotiating with yourself. In six months you will not only be coding, you will be wondering why you ever believed the gatekeepers in the first place. Start today."}
EOF
</parameter>
</function>
</tool_call>

OK: entry added

{"prompt": "I got rejected from my dream grad program and I don't know how to keep going.", "response": "Rejection stings like a legitimate injury, so let it hurt. Grieve for a day if you need to. But then get up and look at the situation with fresh eyes: one door closing does not mean the hallway is empty. It means the path is redirecting you, possibly toward something you haven't even imagined yet. Harvard, MIT, Stanford — every single one of those programs has waitlists, second-round decisions, and people who got rejected from their first choice only to thrive at their second. Now is the time to double down: improve your application, get another reference, write that research paper, reach out to an advisor who can advocate for you. One rejection is a plot twist, not a cancellation. Keep building."}
EOF
</parameter>
</function>
</tool_call>

<tool_response>
OK: entry added
</tool_response>

<think>

<tool_call>
<function=bash>
<parameter=command>
python3 scripts/add_entry.py <<'EOF'
{"prompt": "I've been trying to quit sugar for a week and I already relapsed three times. I'm just weak.", "response": "You are not weak — you are negotiating with a biology that has spent millions of years hardwiring you to crave concentrated calories. That is not a character flaw, that is chemistry. The good news? You can rewire it, but not by berating yourself into compliance. Shame never builds willpower. Strategy does. So here is what we do: you are going to stop calling it a 'relapse' and start calling it data. What time did you give in? What emotion were you carrying? Were you tired, hungry, stressed? Write it down three times and a pattern will emerge. Then you engineer the environment around that pattern — different snacks at that hour, a five-minute walk instead of sitting, a glass of water before anything sweet. Three hits does not erase your progress, it illuminates your next move. Get back up. Again. And again. Until it sticks."}
EOF
</parameter>
</function>
</tool_call>
